intro: Five modules follow the five Linux+ XK0-006 domains and their weights. Each has a study guide, exam tips, key terms, visual slides, and a narrated lesson. Linux+ includes performance-based questions, so pair these modules with the hands-on labs.

modules.title: System management
modules.summary: Understand the boot process, kernel modules and hardware, storage with partitions, LVM, RAID, and file systems, network configuration with NetworkManager and Netplan, shell operations, backups, and virtualization with KVM and libvirt.

guide.html: System management is 23% of XK0-006, the largest domain. It spans seven objectives: Linux basics and boot, devices and kernel modules, storage, network configuration, shell operations, backup and restore, and virtualization.

Boot order: UEFI/BIOS → GRUB 2 → kernel + initramfs → systemd. Change kernel arguments in /etc/default/grub, then regenerate (grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg or update-grub); on RHEL, grubby edits entries directly. Rebuild the initramfs with dracut -f (RHEL) or update-initramfs -u (Debian). Kernel modules: lsmod, modinfo, modprobe (resolves dependencies), modprobe -r; persist with /etc/modules-load.d and blacklist in /etc/modprobe.d. Hardware tools: lspci -k, lsusb, lshw, dmidecode, lscpu, dmesg. Architectures: x86_64, AArch64 (64-bit ARM), RISC-V.

Partition with fdisk, gdisk, or parted (GPT for modern systems). LVM: pvcreate → vgcreate → lvcreate → mkfs; grow with lvextend -r. File systems: ext4 (grow and shrink), XFS (grow only, xfs_growfs), Btrfs (subvolumes, snapshots), tmpfs (RAM). Software RAID with mdadm (check /proc/mdstat). Mount persistently in /etc/fstab by UUID (blkid), test with mount -a or findmnt --verify, and use options like noexec,nosuid,nodev and _netdev for NFS/SMB. Check space with df -h and inodes with df -i.

Network: nmcli con mod/up (NetworkManager), Netplan YAML on Ubuntu (netplan apply), /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/nsswitch.conf; tools ip, ss, dig, ping, tracepath, nc. Shell: environment variables, ~/.bashrc vs ~/.bash_profile, /etc/profile.d, redirection and pipes, and vi/vim and nano basics. Backups: tar, cpio, rsync -a, dd for images, ddrescue for failing disks, and compression with gzip, bzip2, xz, zstd. Virtualization: KVM (kernel module) + QEMU (emulation), managed with libvirt (virsh list --all, start, shutdown, snapshot-create-as), disk images in qcow2 (qemu-img), and NAT, bridged, or isolated networks.

tips: PV → VG → LV → mkfs → mount → fstab; lvextend -r grows the file system too.
XFS can't shrink; ext4 can (offline).
df -i reveals inode exhaustion when space looks free.
modprobe resolves dependencies; insmod doesn't.
Test every fstab change with mount -a before rebooting.
terms: Early RAM file system with drivers needed to mount root.
Tool that builds the initramfs on RHEL-family systems.
Logical Volume Manager: flexible volumes from pooled disks.
Tool that manages Linux software RAID.
Unique file system identifier used in fstab.
QEMU disk image format with thin provisioning and snapshots.

slides.title: System management
script: Welcome to the system management module, the largest Linux+ domain. It's about building and running a Linux server: from boot to disks, networking, backups, and virtual machines.
Many performance-based questions come from this domain, so practice the storage commands in the labs.

slides.title: Boot and kernel modules
script: The firmware loads GRUB, GRUB loads the kernel and initramfs, and the kernel starts systemd.
Change boot arguments in etc default grub and regenerate the config. Load modules with modprobe, and rebuild the initramfs with dracut when early drivers change.

slides.title: Storage with LVM
script: LVM pools disks into volume groups, then carves out logical volumes you can grow later.
Create physical volumes, a volume group, and a logical volume, then make a file system and mount it by UUID in fstab.

slides.title: Mounts and file systems
script: Every persistent mount goes in fstab: device, mount point, type, options, dump, and fsck order. Use UUIDs so device renames don't break boot.
When writes fail but space looks free, check inodes with df dash i.

slides.title: Network configuration
script: NetworkManager profiles are changed with nmcli con mod and activated with nmcli con up. Ubuntu servers use Netplan YAML files.
Name resolution follows nsswitch.conf: usually etc hosts first, then the DNS servers in resolv.conf.

slides.title: Backups and virtualization
script: Use tar for archives, rsync for efficient copies, and dd for exact disk images.
KVM and QEMU run virtual machines, libvirt manages them with virsh, and qcow2 images support thin provisioning and snapshots.

slides.title: Review: system management
script: You've finished the system management module. Go back over the key terms and commands, and try them in the labs.
Then take the system management question set. Linux+ includes performance-based questions, so hands-on practice matters.

modules.title: Services and user management
modules.summary: Manage files and links, local accounts and password aging, processes, jobs, and scheduling, software packages and repositories, common network services, systemd units, and containers with Podman and Docker.

guide.html: Services and user management is 20% of XK0-006: files and directories, local accounts, processes and jobs, software configuration, systemd, and containers.

useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G wheel name, usermod -aG, usermod -L (lock), userdel -r, groupadd. System/service accounts: useradd -r -s /sbin/nologin. Password aging with chage (-M max days, -d 0 force change, -E expiry, -l list); defaults in /etc/login.defs; templates in /etc/skel. Files: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group, /etc/gshadow.

Inspect with ps -ef, ps aux --sort=-%cpu, top/htop, pstree, pgrep, lsof. States: R running, S sleeping, D uninterruptible (I/O), Z zombie, T stopped. Signals: SIGTERM 15 (default), SIGKILL 9, SIGHUP 1 (reload), SIGINT 2 (Ctrl+C). Priority: nice -n starts, renice -n N -p PID changes (-20 highest, 19 lowest). Jobs: &, Ctrl+Z, bg, fg, jobs, nohup. Scheduling: crontab -e (min hour dom mon dow), at for one-time jobs, anacron for machines that are off at night, and systemd timers.

Package tools: dnf/rpm (RHEL, Fedora), apt/dpkg (Debian, Ubuntu), zypper (SUSE). Repositories live in /etc/yum.repos.d/ or /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ and are verified by GPG keys. Find owners: rpm -qf, dnf provides, dpkg -S. update-alternatives picks default versions. Know basic service roles: DNS (BIND), NTP/PTP (chrony, linuxptp), DHCP, HTTP (httpd, NGINX), SMTP (Postfix), IMAP (Dovecot).

Unit types: service, timer, mount, target, socket. systemctl start/stop/restart/reload/enable/disable/mask/status, systemctl daemon-reload after editing units, systemctl edit for drop-ins, systemctl list-timers, systemd-analyze blame. Helpers: hostnamectl, timedatectl, resolvectl. Containers: podman/docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 -v data:/path image, ps, logs, exec, stop, rm, images, pull, build -t from a Containerfile (FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD). Podman runs rootless by default; add :Z to bind mounts on SELinux hosts.

tips: usermod -aG appends; -G alone replaces supplementary groups.
chage -d 0 forces a password change at next login.
Cron fields: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week.
Port mapping is -p host:container.
Run systemctl daemon-reload after editing unit files.
terms: Template files copied into new home directories.
Exited process whose parent hasn't collected its status.
Runs periodic jobs that were missed while the system was off.
A systemd object: service, timer, mount, target, socket.
systemd's scheduled trigger for a service.
Container run by an unprivileged user.
Persistent storage managed by the container runtime.

slides.title: Services and users
script: This module covers the day-to-day work of running services and supporting users.
You'll manage accounts and password policy, processes and schedules, packages, systemd units, and containers.

slides.title: Accounts and password aging
script: Create users with useradd, add groups with usermod dash a capital G, and lock departing users with usermod dash capital L.
chage sets password aging per user, and login.defs sets defaults for new accounts. Service accounts get a nologin shell.

slides.title: Processes and jobs
bullets: States: R S D Z T
script: ps and top show process states. D means waiting on I/O, Z means zombie.
Send signals with kill, adjust priority with renice, background jobs with bg, and schedule with cron, at, anacron, or systemd timers.

slides.title: Packages and repositories
bullets: Find which package owns a file
script: Install software from repositories, which are signed with GPG keys so you can trust their packages.
Use rpm dash q f or dnf provides on Red Hat systems, and dpkg dash capital S on Debian, to find which package provides a file.

slides.title: systemd units and timers
script: systemd manages units. Enable a service to start it at boot, and use timers instead of cron when you want logging and catch-up runs.
After editing a unit file, run daemon reload. Mask a unit to stop anything from starting it.

slides.title: Containers
script: Containers package an application with its dependencies. Build images from a Containerfile with FROM, RUN, COPY, and CMD.
Run them with ports mapped host to container and data in volumes so it survives when the container is removed.

slides.title: Review: services and user management
script: You've finished the services and user management module. Go back over the key terms and commands, and try them in the labs.
Then take the services and user management question set. Linux+ includes performance-based questions, so hands-on practice matters.

modules.title: Security
modules.summary: Harden the OS and accounts, control privilege with sudo, permissions, ACLs, and SELinux or AppArmor, authenticate with PAM, SSSD, LDAP, and Kerberos, configure firewalls, apply cryptography, and support compliance and auditing.

guide.html: Security is 18% of XK0-006: OS hardening, authentication/authorization/accounting, firewalls, account hardening, cryptography, and compliance and audit.

Grant least privilege with sudo rules in /etc/sudoers.d/, always edited with visudo. Permissions and special bits (SUID 4, SGID 2, sticky 1), umask (027 → files 640, dirs 750), ACLs (setfacl -m u:name:rw, getfacl), and file attributes (chattr +i immutable, +a append-only). Mandatory access control: SELinux (RHEL; getenforce, contexts, booleans) or AppArmor (Ubuntu, SUSE; profiles). SSH: PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no, AllowGroups, test with sshd -t. Replace Telnet/FTP/HTTP logins with encrypted protocols. Secure Boot verifies signed bootloaders and kernels.

PAM (/etc/pam.d) stacks modules such as pam_pwquality (password rules), pam_faillock (lockout; pam_tally2 is legacy), and MFA modules. SSSD joins hosts to LDAP or Active Directory (realm join) with Kerberos; Winbind is the Samba alternative. polkit authorizes privileged desktop/system actions. Accounting: journalctl, rsyslog, logrotate, and auditd rules (auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p wa, ausearch, aureport).

firewalld (firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https, then --reload), ufw (ufw default deny incoming, ufw allow OpenSSH, ufw enable), and the underlying nftables (successor to iptables); ipset for address sets. Stateful filtering tracks connections. Routing and NAT need net.ipv4.ip_forward=1. Crypto: LUKS2 disk encryption (cryptsetup luksFormat/open, /etc/crypttab), GPG for files, OpenSSL for certificates (openssl x509 -noout -enddate), TLS 1.2/1.3 only, WireGuard VPN, SHA-256 hashes, and system crypto policies on RHEL.

Scan against benchmarks with OpenSCAP (CIS, STIG profiles); detect file changes with AIDE; check for rootkits with rkhunter; prioritize patches using CVE IDs and CVSS scores; destroy data securely (shred, secure erase, crypto-erase); verify software supply chains with signatures; and display legal login banners in /etc/issue, /etc/issue.net, and sshd's Banner.

tips: Edit sudoers only with visudo; prefer drop-ins in /etc/sudoers.d.
umask 027 → new files 640, directories 750.
firewall-cmd changes are runtime unless you add --permanent (then --reload).
pam_faillock replaces pam_tally2 on current distributions.
CVE identifies a vulnerability; CVSS scores its severity.
terms: Access control list: per-user or per-group permissions on a file.
Label-based mandatory access control used by RHEL.
Path-based mandatory access control used by Ubuntu and SUSE.
Service that connects Linux to LDAP/AD identity sources.
Kernel audit daemon that records security events.
Tool that scans systems against security profiles.

slides.title: Security
script: This module covers securing a Linux server: limiting privileges, authenticating users, filtering traffic, encrypting data, and proving compliance.
Expect scenario questions that ask for the most secure option that still meets the requirement.

slides.title: Least privilege
script: Give people only the commands they need with sudo rules, edited safely with visudo.
Set sensible default permissions with umask, use ACLs for exceptions, lock critical files with chattr, and let SELinux or AppArmor confine services.

slides.title: Hardening SSH
script: SSH is the front door of most servers. Disable root login and password authentication so only key holders get in.
Restrict who can connect with AllowGroups, validate the config with sshd dash t, and then restart the service.

slides.title: Authentication and logging
script: PAM decides how users authenticate: password quality, lockouts, and MFA are all PAM modules.
SSSD connects to directories like Active Directory. Logs and audit rules record what happened so you can investigate.

slides.title: Firewalls
script: firewalld groups rules into zones. Changes are runtime only unless you add dash dash permanent and reload.
Ubuntu uses ufw: default deny incoming, allow SSH, then enable. Both build on nftables.

slides.title: Cryptography and compliance
script: Encrypt disks with LUKS2, files with GPG, and connections with TLS 1.2 or 1.3. Check certificates with openssl.
Prove compliance by scanning with OpenSCAP, watching file integrity with AIDE, and patching by CVSS severity.

slides.title: Review: security
script: You've finished the security module. Go back over the key terms and commands, and try them in the labs.
Then take the security question set. Linux+ includes performance-based questions, so hands-on practice matters.

modules.title: Automation, orchestration, and scripting
modules.summary: Automate with infrastructure as code and configuration management, orchestrate containers, write robust Bash scripts, use Python basics and Git, apply AI tools responsibly, and monitor services against service levels.

guide.html: Automation, orchestration, and scripting is 17% of XK0-006: IaC and orchestration, shell scripting, Python basics, Git, AI best practices, and monitoring.

Ansible is agentless and pushes over SSH using YAML playbooks (hosts, tasks, modules, handlers, roles, inventory). Puppet agents pull manifests from a server. OpenTofu/Terraform provision infrastructure declaratively. All aim for idempotence: running twice changes nothing the second time. Kickstart automates RHEL installs; cloud-init configures cloud instances at first boot. CI/CD pipelines build and test every change. Containers are orchestrated by Kubernetes (pods, deployments, services), Docker Swarm, or Compose files for small multi-container apps.

Start with #!/bin/bash and consider set -euo pipefail. Variables and expansion (${var:-default}, ${#var}, ${file%.txt}), command substitution $(...), arithmetic $((...)). Tests: [ -f ], [ -d ], string =, numeric -eq -lt -gt, and [[ ]] with regex =~. Control flow: if/elif/else/fi, case ... esac, for, while read -r line, until. Functions: name() { ...; } with return. Exit codes: $?, exit N, &&, ||. IFS controls word splitting; awk's OFS sets output separators.

Python: isolate dependencies with python3 -m venv and pip install -r requirements.txt; know data types (str, int, list, tuple, dict, set), built-in modules (os, sys, subprocess, json, pathlib), and PEP 8 style. Git: clone, add, commit, push, pull, branch, switch -c, merge, rebase, stash, tag, log, diff, and .gitignore. AI: review and test generated code, protect secrets and personal data, follow company policy, and write specific prompts. Monitoring: SLIs measure, SLOs set targets, SLAs are agreements; collect with agents or agentlessly (SNMP), alert on thresholds, and send webhooks.

tips: Ansible = agentless push over SSH; Puppet = agent pull.
Idempotent tasks can run repeatedly without extra changes.
Quote variables: "$var"; use [ ] tests with spaces inside the brackets.
git switch -c creates and switches to a new branch.
SLI = measurement, SLO = target, SLA = agreement.
terms: Applying the same configuration again causes no further change.
Ansible YAML file of plays and tasks.
Replays commits on top of another branch.
Target value for a service-level indicator.

slides.title: Automation and scripting
script: This module is about doing work once and letting tools repeat it: infrastructure as code, configuration management, scripts, and version control.
Linux+ V8 also adds responsible AI use and monitoring concepts.

slides.title: Configuration management
script: Ansible connects over SSH without agents and runs YAML playbooks against hosts in an inventory. Puppet agents pull configuration from a server.
Both are idempotent: they describe the desired state and change only what's different.

slides.title: Robust Bash scripts
script: Good scripts fail loudly. set dash e u o pipefail stops on errors, unset variables, and failed pipelines.
Use tests, case statements, loops, and functions, and return meaningful exit codes so other tools can react.

slides.title: Python and Git
script: Use a virtual environment for every Python project so its packages don't break system tools.
Track scripts and playbooks in Git: branch for each change, commit with clear messages, and merge or rebase when ready.

slides.title: AI and monitoring
script: AI assistants can draft scripts, but you're responsible for reviewing and testing them, and you must never paste secrets or private data into prompts.
Monitoring turns metrics into alerts: SLIs measure, SLOs set targets, and thresholds trigger notifications.

slides.title: Review: automation and scripting
script: You've finished the automation and scripting module. Go back over the key terms and commands, and try them in the labs.
Then take the automation and scripting question set. Linux+ includes performance-based questions, so hands-on practice matters.

modules.title: Troubleshooting
modules.summary: Diagnose and fix boot, storage, and service failures, network problems from DNS to MTU, security issues such as SELinux denials and permission errors, and performance bottlenecks in CPU, memory, disk, and network.

guide.html: Troubleshooting is 22% of XK0-006: hardware, storage, and OS issues; networking; security; and performance. Questions describe symptoms and ask for the most likely cause or the best next command.

A bad /etc/fstab line drops the system to emergency mode; fix it, then mount -a. Full disks: df -h, then du -xh | sort -h; space held by deleted-but-open files shows with lsof +L1; inode exhaustion shows with df -i. Quotas: quota, repquota, xfs_quota. Kernel panic after an update: boot the previous kernel from GRUB. A grub> prompt means a broken GRUB config. Failed units: systemctl status, journalctl -u name -b. Missing drivers: lspci -k, dmesg. Memory leaks end with the OOM killer (journalctl -k | grep -i oom).

Work up the stack: link (ip link, ethtool), address and gateway (ip addr, ip route), name resolution (dig, resolvectl, /etc/hosts), firewall (firewall-cmd --list-all, nft list ruleset), and the service (ss -tlnp; listening on 127.0.0.1 only means remote clients can't connect). Large transfers stalling suggests MTU problems (ping -M do -s 1400). IP conflicts show with arping -D. Use tcpdump, mtr, and tracepath to see where traffic stops. In dual-stack networks, check IPv6 routes too.

Security: SELinux denials (ausearch -m AVC -ts recent, sealert) are fixed with correct labels (semanage fcontext + restorecon), port labels, or booleans, not by disabling SELinux. Permission problems: check the path's execute bits, group membership (log in again), and ACL masks. Account issues: passwd -S, chage -l, faillock. Certificates: expired, wrong name, or missing intermediate chain. Performance: high wa in top means I/O wait (iostat -x, iotop); high load with high CPU means a CPU bottleneck (ps --sort=-%cpu); swapping and OOM point to memory (free -h, vmstat); sar compares with a baseline.

tips: Emergency mode after reboot? Suspect /etc/fstab first.
df full but du can't find it: a deleted file is still open (lsof +L1).
Can ping by IP but not by name: DNS.
Works locally, not remotely: firewall or listening address.
High wa = I/O wait; check iostat and iotop.
terms: Minimal boot target when required mounts or units fail.
Kernel mechanism that kills a process when memory runs out.
Metadata record for one file; each file system has a fixed number (ext4).
Largest packet size a link carries without fragmentation.
SELinux log entry for a blocked action.
CPU time spent waiting on storage.
Average number of runnable or waiting processes.
Normal performance values to compare against.

slides.title: Troubleshooting
script: The troubleshooting domain is about reasoning from symptoms. For each scenario, ask what changed, what the evidence shows, and which command confirms it.
This module gives you the patterns that show up again and again.

slides.title: Boot and storage problems
script: Most failed boots after a change come from fstab. Fix the line from emergency mode and test with mount dash a.
When a disk looks full, compare df and du, check inodes, and look for deleted files still held open.

slides.title: Network troubleshooting
script: Work from the bottom up: is the link up, is the address and gateway right, does DNS resolve, is the firewall open, and is the service listening on the right address?
If small packets work but big transfers stall, test the MTU.

slides.title: Security problems
script: When SELinux blocks something, read the denial and fix the label, port, or boolean. Never leave SELinux disabled.
For permission errors, check every directory on the path, group membership, and ACLs. For logins, check locks, expiry, and faillock.

slides.title: Performance
script: High load with busy CPUs points to CPU. High wa points to storage. Heavy swapping and OOM kills point to memory.
Measure with top, vmstat, iostat, and sar, and compare against a baseline so you know what normal looks like.

slides.title: Review: troubleshooting
script: You've finished the troubleshooting module. Go back over the key terms and commands, and try them in the labs.
Then take the troubleshooting question set. Linux+ includes performance-based questions, so hands-on practice matters.
